text: Human sacrifice was a Celtic ritual. Roman sources say both the continental and the insular Celts practiced it. Julius Caesar described one rite. Victims and scores of animals were trapped in a gigantic figure made of wicker, then burned alive. Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, and Tacitus agree the Celts offered human beings to their gods. Tacitus said the Druids covered their altars with the blood of captives and consulted the gods through entrails. He used this to explain the Roman attack on the sanctuary at Anglesey. Later writers, more friendly to the Celts, said the Romans slandered them. Current evidence suggests sacrifice did happen, though not regularly. It may have been an old form of capital punishment, kept for criminals and prisoners. The Celts believed in reincarnation, so a human death carried a different weight for them. Bog bodies, such as the Lindow Man, show signs of the threefold death of strangling, cutting, and drowning. The myth of Conaire, burned in Da Derga's hostel, supports the practice.

okr.objective: Document Celtic human sacrifice as reported by Roman writers and seen in bog bodies.
